title: The P Feature Zoo
takeaway: One coarse feature that looked like a pointless "fires on the letter P" detector turns out, in wider dictionaries, to be a family of sixteen or more features that each fire on P in a different context — surnames, acronym patterns, biochemistry, LaTeX, legal citations. The paper offers this as its explanation for the strange single-token features that show up in small dictionaries: they are contexts the small dictionary could not tell apart, so widening the dictionary refines them rather than fragmenting them.
walkthrough:
### What the columns are

Five columns, one per [[dictionary-learning-run]] in the A sequence, from A/0 with 512 learned features to A/4 with 65,536.

All five [[sparse-autoencoder]] runs are trained on activations from the same one-layer transformer, with the same sparsity setting. Only the dictionary size changes. So the columns are five resolutions of one underlying picture, which is what the paper means by treating [[dictionary-resolution]] as a zoom level.

Each dark box names one feature in the paper's [[feature-notation]] — run, then index within that run. The grey text below is the authors' reading of what that feature fires on. Every feature shown fires on the token " P" where a word begins with a capital P; [[byte-pair-encoding]] makes that a token in its own right.

### How to read the links

A line joins a feature to its relatives one column over. Where several features connect, the lines merge into one vertical spine, so a bundle says the family carries over without saying which parent became which child.

Two cautions. The paper notes these P relatives were found by manual inspection, not by the [[masked-cosine-similarity]] score used in the mathematics-and-physics figure — so the links here are a hand-drawn reading, not a measured one. And the relation is not a clean tree anyway: [[splitting-is-not-a-tree]] is the paper's own statement that features both split and merge between sizes.

### What it shows

At A/0 there is a single box, A/0/395, "Misc. 'P' Feature", with a list of P-words. At A/1, still one. That is the apparent bug: a high-magnitude feature that fires on one token and seems to add nothing a bigram could not supply.

At A/2 it has become four: a leftover misc feature, surnames starting with P, P\*N\* acronyms, and PDE. At A/3 there are ten, at A/4 sixteen — Pokemon, PCB, PPAR, PEG, LaTeX $P\_\{$, the legal citation "P.".

The claim is that [[feature-splitting]] refines rather than fragments: the coarse feature was already covering all these contexts at once, and the specific ones are [[token-in-context-features]]. This fits the paper's conjecture about [[true-features]] held in tight [[superposition]]. The evidence here is the labels themselves, which are summaries of activating examples; no quantitative check appears in this figure.

terms.definition: The leftmost column header: the coarsest dictionary learning run on transformer A, with 512 learned features. It is the same width as the MLP layer being decomposed, so it has no room to spare.
The second column: the 4,096-feature run, which is the dictionary the paper analyses in most detail elsewhere. In this figure it still holds only one P feature.
The middle column: the 16,384-feature run. It is where the single P feature first visibly divides.
The fourth column: the 32,768-feature run. Ten P features are drawn here.
The rightmost column: the 65,536-feature run, the widest dictionary shown. Sixteen P features are drawn here.

The paper's identifier for a single learned feature: transformer (A), dictionary learning run (0–4), then the feature's index inside that run. The index carries no meaning beyond position in the dictionary.

The authors' label for a feature that fires on the token " P" across assorted words with no narrower pattern they could name. It is the coarse, unsplit form of the whole family, and it survives in reduced form even at A/4.

terms.term: Bolded P in the word lists
terms.definition: A typographic convention in the figure: within each example word, the P the feature actually fires on is bold. It marks that the activating unit is the token " P", not the whole word.

terms.term: Plastic, Possibly, Pioneer, Preliminary, Pseud-, Pregn(ant), Prairie, Patterns, Pension, Peking, Pseudo, Pulse
terms.definition: The example words listed under A/0/395 and A/1/1057. They are unrelated in meaning, which is the point: at these dictionary sizes the feature's only common thread is the letter itself.

terms.term: Ponce, PIPER, Pichon, Pell, Pioneer, Possibilities, Pronounciation, PNAS, PSA
terms.definition: The examples under A/2/7661, the misc P feature that survives into A/2. The mix of names, ordinary words and acronyms shows this box is still the unresolved residue. "Pronounciation" is printed with that spelling in the figure.

terms.term: First letter of last name, esp. beginning in P (Pabst, Pugh, Pays, Pryon, Pates, Pattinson)
terms.definition: The reading of A/2/7573: a feature that fires on the initial P of surnames rather than on P generally. It is one of the first genuinely contextual splits.

terms.term: Acronyms, esp. P*N* (PN, PNs, PNN, PPN, PND, PNP)
terms.definition: The reading of A/2/4318: a feature for P-initial acronyms whose following letters tend to include N. The asterisks are wildcards standing for any letters, so P*N* is a rough pattern rather than a strict string.

The same wildcard shorthand for sibling acronym features at A/3 and A/4 — A/3/32708 and A/4/49203 for P*V*, A/3/9092 for P*W*, and the P*E* note on the A/2 math/protein box. Each covers a different letter pattern inside P-initial acronyms.

The reading of A/2/4318, A/3/22720 and A/4/32210: a feature firing on the token P in the acronym PDE, which reads as "partial differential equation" in mathematics and "phosphodiesterase" in biology. The label keeps both because the feature does not separate them.
An additional acronym listed under A/3/22720 alongside PDE. In chemistry it names polybrominated diphenyl ethers; the figure lists it as a token the feature also fires on.
The reading of A/3/7399: a feature for the acronym PLD plus a grab-bag of other P-initial acronyms. This box is drawn as the parent of the boxed cluster of seven narrow A/4 features.
The reading of A/3/6439 and A/4/41489: a feature firing on P in PCB, printed circuit board, in electronics writing. It is one of the pairs joined by a single straight line across the two columns.
The reading of A/3/7313 and A/4/27099: a feature that fires on the P of Pokemon. It is a case where the split lands on one proper noun rather than a topic.
The reading of A/3/8618 and A/4/4598: a feature for the P in PPAR, a receptor protein family, in biochemical text.
The reading of A/3/20260 and A/4/12546: a feature for the P in PEG, polyethylene glycol.
The reading of A/4/32210 inside the boxed cluster: a feature for the P in cytochrome P450, a family of enzymes. It appears only at the widest dictionary size shown.
The reading of A/4/13120: a feature for the P in the journal name PLOS (Public Library of Science), in both capitalisations.
The reading of A/4/22642: a feature for the P of "Pitt", covering the university and the surname without distinguishing them.
The reading of A/4/29469: a feature for the P in PPI and assorted other acronyms. The "other acronyms" tail means even at 65,536 features some boxes remain partly unresolved.
The reading of A/4/43583: a feature firing on the P of a specific two-word organisation name. It is the narrowest kind of split shown.
The reading of A/4/10255: a feature for P in LaTeX markup, where it is followed by subscript or superscript syntax. The context is a typesetting format rather than a subject area.
The reading of A/4/16535: a feature for the abbreviation "P." as it appears in legal citations. The same character carries a different role here than in prose.

terms.term: PNAS, PSA, PLR, PZQ, PV, PBD
terms.definition: Assorted acronym tokens listed under the misc features A/2/7661 and A/3/2303. The figure gives them as raw examples without expansions; they are there to show these boxes are still mixed rather than to name particular topics.

terms.term: The rounded box grouping seven A/4 features
terms.definition: A thin outline enclosing A/4/22642, 13120, 32210, 16535, 29469, 43583 and 10255. It marks them as one cluster of narrow acronym-and-name features sharing a link back into the A/3 column, so the drawing does not have to run seven separate lines.

terms.term: Connecting lines and the vertical spine
terms.definition: Lines join a feature to its relatives in the neighbouring column. Where several connect, the lines join a shared vertical bar, which shows family membership across the two runs but not which individual feature descends from which.
The paper's name for what this figure shows: as the dictionary is made wider, one feature is replaced by several more specific features covering roughly the same territory.

The similarity score the paper uses elsewhere to link a feature to its relatives across runs, computed over only the tokens where at least one of the two fires. The text states it was not used here — the P relatives were found by manual inspection instead.

Each of these two identifiers is printed on two different boxes with different descriptions — A/2/4318 as both the P*N* acronym feature and the math/protein feature, A/4/32210 as both P450 and PDE. The paper does not comment; read as printed, it is most likely a labelling slip in the diagram.

numbers.meaning: The dictionary size of run A/0. It equals the number of neurons in the MLP layer being decomposed, an expansion factor of 1×, so this dictionary has exactly as many features as the layer has neurons and no capacity to separate contexts.
The dictionary size of run A/1, an 8× expansion. This is the run the paper analyses in most depth elsewhere, and here it is still coarse enough that only one P feature exists.
The dictionary size of run A/2, a 32× expansion. The figure shows the P family first dividing at this width.
The dictionary size of run A/3, a 64× expansion, twice A/2.
The dictionary size of run A/4, a 128× expansion, twice A/3 and the widest run in this figure.

The number of P-feature boxes drawn in each column, left to right. Doubling the dictionary from A/3 to A/4 does not double the family, and the growth is what the paper points at rather than any exact count — this is a hand-assembled diagram, not an exhaustive census.
The size of A/5, the next run in the same sequence and a 256× expansion. It lies beyond this figure's rightmost column, so the splitting shown here is not the end of the sequence.

The masked cosine similarity threshold above which the paper draws a link between features in the neighbouring mathematics-and-physics figure, chosen to keep that graph small enough to read. It does not apply here: the text says these P relatives were identified manually.
Part of the enzyme family name cytochrome P450, from the wavelength in nanometres at which the pigment absorbs. It is a fragment of a token string, not a measurement the paper made.

Numbers from the companion example in the same section, where one base64 feature in A/0 splits into three in A/1. They are not in this figure but are the paper's other worked case of the same splitting claim.

Arbitrary positions inside each dictionary, running from 0 up to the run's size minus one. An index in the tens of thousands can only come from A/3 or A/4, which is a quick consistency check on the labels; the numbers carry no ordering or importance.
